You asked straight, so: yes, I think it was broadly the right decision — but it was closer than your brother-in-law's tone implies, and the No side's arguments weren't wrong. They just lost.

The strongest reason I lean yes: the old system was constitutionally dead on arrival. The Federal Court ruled joint taxation of couples unconstitutional back in 1984 — the Heiratsstrafe case — and gave Parliament five years to fix it. Forty years later, hundreds of thousands of dual-earner couples were still paying more than if they'd simply lived together unmarried. When the legislature fails that long, a party reaching for the initiative tool is exactly what direct democracy is for. And taxing each spouse individually is the cleaner principle: your tax bill no longer depends on a marriage certificate, and splitting no longer hits the second (usually lower) earner's income with a brutal marginal rate.

That said, the No case had real substance, and I'd take it seriously even after the vote:

- Single-earner couples lose splitting and will pay meaningfully more — effectively a tax increase on a family model that produces untaxed care work at home. If you think the state should recognize that work, No was principled.
- The 50/50 split of capital income is a blunt anti-avoidance rule.
- The initiative pre-empted the more finely balanced counter-project Parliament was still drafting, and froze details into the constitution that arguably belonged in legislation.

So this wasn't right versus wrong; it was a value weighting. Mine just tips toward fixing a forty-year constitutional defect with a clear principle rather than waiting for a perfect compromise that never arrived.

Two other things worth saying. First, "the people have spoken, deal with it" is procedurally true — 54 percent plus the cantonal majority settles the legal question — but it's the weakest form of the argument. Ballots settle outcomes, not merit; 46 percent don't owe anyone a concession, and Swiss history is full of winning majorities later proven wrong. Second, the real fight now moves to the implementing law: deductions for children and care costs, transition rules, cantonal alignment — probably not in force before around 2028. Whether this turns out well depends far more on that legislation than on the March result. That's where a No-voter's attention — and maybe a well-aimed letter in the consultation process — is better spent than in relitigating the vote.

One last, unglamorous point: whether you personally come out ahead depends mostly on how income is split between you and your spouse, not on ideology. Which is, roughly, how the country split too.

You asked straight, so: yes, I think it was broadly the right decision — but it's closer than your brother-in-law's smugness implies, and the No side's arguments weren't wrong. They just lost.

The strongest reason I lean Yes: the old system was constitutionally dead on arrival. The Federal Court ruled joint taxation of couples unconstitutional in 1984 — that's the Heiratsstrafe case — and gave Parliament five years to fix it. Forty years later, hundreds of thousands of dual-earner couples were still paying more than if they'd simply lived together unmarried. When Parliament fails for four decades, a party reaching for the initiative tool is what direct democracy is for. And individually taxing each spouse is the cleaner principle: your tax bill no longer depends on a marriage certificate, and splitting no longer punishes the second (usually lower) earner's income with a brutal marginal rate.

That said, the No case had real substance, and I'd take it seriously even after the vote:

- Single-earner couples lose splitting and will pay meaningfully more. That's a tax increase on a family model that generates untaxed care work at home. If you think the state should recognize that work, No was principled.
- The 50/50 split of capital income is a blunt anti-avoidance rule.
- The initiative pre-empted the more finely balanced counter-project Parliament was still drafting, and froze details into the constitution that should have been legislated.

So this wasn't right-vs-wrong; it was a value weighting. My own weighting just tips toward fixing a 40-year constitutional defect with a clear principle rather than waiting for a perfect compromise that never arrived.

Two other things worth saying. First, "the people have spoken, deal with it" is procedurally true — 54 percent plus a cantonal majority ends the legal argument — but it's the weakest form of the argument. Ballots settle outcomes, not merit; 46 percent don't owe anyone a concession, and Swiss history is full of winning majorities later proven wrong (the women's vote took until 1971). Second, the real game is now the implementing law: deductions for children and care costs, transition rules, cantonal alignment — probably in force around 2028. Whether this turns out well depends far more on that legislation than on the March result. That's where a No-voter's attention — and maybe a well-aimed consultation letter — is better spent than in relitigating the vote.
